summary: Adds explanation, examples and guidance to the revised Expedited Forwarding definition in RFC 3246, written during clarification of the older RFC 2598. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is the extra homework help for the fast-lane rules, with examples that explain why they are written that way.

questions: why was rfc 2598 ef definition replaced
what is the ef latency term
subtitle: Extra explanation, examples and scheduler guidance for the revised Expedited Forwarding definition.

tldr.problem: The original EF PHB definition in RFC 2598 was not precise enough, and even sensible forwarders such as a perfectly clocked one or one with internal delay could not formally comply.
tldr.mechanism: The revised definition uses two sets of equations, one for the EF aggregate and one aware of packet identity, each with a configured rate R and an error term. This RFC explains them and shows how to compute the error terms for several schedulers.
tldr.outcome: It adds explanation only, no new functions, and supports the revised EF definition in RFC 3246.

today: RFC 3247 is an Informational memo from March 2002, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It supplements the revised EF definition in RFC 3246, which replaced the older wording of RFC 2598.

sections.title: Purpose of the Supplement
sections.content:
The Expedited Forwarding (EF) Per-Hop Behavior was designed to build a low-loss, low-latency, low-jitter, assured bandwidth service. Because it is so valuable, the behavior required of an EF-compliant node needs to be specific, quantifiable and unambiguous.

The definition in the original RFC 2598 was not precise enough. A more precise one is given in RFC 3246, and this document aids understanding of it with material left out there for brevity: discussion of the definition, per-packet delay, packet loss, and the effect of known scheduler designs on the key parameters.
sections.eli5: The fast-lane rule needs to be exact so everyone builds it the same way. This note explains the exact version.

sections.title: Problems With the RFC 2598 Definition
sections.content:
Appendix A shows why the old wording failed. A literal reading says EF traffic should average at least the configured rate over any interval as long as the time to send one MTU-sized packet at that rate.

  • Perfectly clocked forwarding: with R = C/2 and an EF packet every other slot, no work-conserving scheduler could formally comply, because the stream arrives at exactly the rate it is served and has no backlog.
  • Router internal delay: with an internal delay of 3T (where T = MTU/C), the EF aggregate is constantly backlogged yet the output rate stays below the configured rate.
  • Maximum rate: with a non-preemptive scheduler the compliant configured rate cannot exceed C/2, and for other schedulers it can be far lower. Even a TDM circuit could not be booked above 50%.

Simple fixes such as averaging over a longer time or counting only backlogged periods did not solve all of these cases.
sections.eli5: The old rule was so strict that even a perfectly fair traffic cop could be called a rule breaker for doing the right thing.

sections.title: The Revised Definition
sections.content:
The RFC restates the formal definition from RFC 3246. A node supporting EF on interface I at a configured rate R MUST satisfy two sets of equations, each with an error term.

  • Aggregate version (E_a): the actual departure time d_j of the j-th EF packet to depart must be no later than a target time f_j plus E_a. A node MUST be characterized by its supported R values and the E_a it can meet.
  • Packet-identity-aware version (E_p): the same shape, but tracking the individual packet that arrived j-th. A node SHOULD be characterized by its R values and E_p, and E_p MAY be given as undefined.

Lengths are measured on the IP datagram, with no lower layer overhead, and the last bit includes any layer 2 trailer. There is also a recommendation that an EF node SHOULD NOT reorder packets within a microflow. The target time uses min(d_(j-1), f_(j-1)), which resets the ideal finish time if a packet left early, so an aggregate is not punished for being served faster than its rate earlier on.
sections.eli5: There are two scorecards: one checks if the whole group of fast-lane packets gets enough speed, the other checks that each packet is not held up too long.

sections.title: Why Two Characterizations
sections.content:
For an ideal output-buffered device with an EF FIFO, the i-th packet in is the i-th out, so E_a = E_p. The definition is then stronger than the well-known rate-latency curve, which can leave long gaps in service after an aggregate was earlier served faster than R.

When the scheduler is not FIFO, or internal delay reorders packets, the two differ. The aggregate version measures how accurately the whole aggregate is served. A small E_a alone says nothing about per-packet delay, since a subset of packets could be delayed arbitrarily if input exceeds the configured rate. The packet-identity-aware version gives a per-packet delay bound as a function of input traffic parameters.

A large E_p does not necessarily mean poor service: a flow-aware scheduler may reorder inside the aggregate and still keep order and low jitter per flow. A small E_p indicates a high quality FIFO implementation. The two terms should be considered together.
sections.eli5: One scorecard asks whether the whole lane moves fast enough. The other asks whether each car waited too long. You need both to judge the road.

sections.title: Delay and Loss
sections.content:
If all traffic into output port I fits a leaky bucket with rate R and depth B, the delay of any packet is bounded by D_p = B/R + E_p. Both R and B should be visible to users of the device. The bound across h hops is not simply h times the single-hop bound unless B is the worst-case burstiness across all nodes. With a shared EF FIFO, jitter can accumulate, so limiting end-to-end delay may need topology constraints as well as limits on EF utilization.

For loss, a node can be described by a token bucket of rate r no more than R and burst size B that can be offered without loss. Conformance must still be checkable when packets are lost: observe the traffic, treat packets that did not leave as removed from the input, and test the equations on the rest. Which packets are dropped is outside the definition.
sections.eli5: How long a car waits depends on how big a crowd shows up at once and how fast the lane moves. Many lanes in a row can make crowds bigger.

sections.title: Scheduler Examples
sections.content:
Extra delays inside a router, such as header processing, a transmission queue or contention in a multi-stage switch core, can be absorbed into the latency terms E_a and E_p. The RFC works two models.

In an ideal output-buffered node with one EF FIFO, E_a = E_p = E and the scheduler sets E. A strict non-preemptive priority queue gives E = MTU/C. A class-based WF2Q gives E = MTU/C + MTU/R. For Deficit Round Robin, E grows linearly with N*(r_max/r_min)*MTU. For Start-Time and Self-Clocked Fair Queuing, E grows linearly with the number of queues.

For a router with internal delay whose variable part is at most D, and an output scheduler with latency E(S), the RFC gives E_p = E(S) + 2D + 2B/R. Without a bound on B it gives E_p = E(S) + D*C_inp/R. Appendix B restates both definitions in an equivalent algebraic form, with proofs in a cited paper.
sections.eli5: Different ways of picking the next car give different waits. The simplest priority lane has a very short wait, while some fair-sharing methods wait longer as more lanes are added.

viz.caption: AGGREGATE EF EQUATIONS RESTATED FROM THE RFC

data.title: Aggregate definition (eq_1, eq_2)
data.code:
d_j <= f_j + E_a                      for all j > 0
f_0 = 0, d_0 = 0
f_j = max(a_j, min(d_j-1, f_j-1)) + l_j/R

viz.caption: LATENCY TERM E FOR OUTPUT-BUFFERED SCHEDULERS

cells: Grows linearly with number of queues
